title: Measure The Market You Actually Compete In
documentTitle: Email from Jonathan Bellack to Eisar Lipkovitz et al. re: DVAA Sellside Review: Jedi++ Strategy
excerptForBlog: I think for the pricing & strategy we should try to separate the GDN part of AdX from the rest. Pubs see GDN as a kind of giant standing demand pool. It is valuable but you can't do deals with it or really game it much because no bid landscapes etc. GDN is half of AdX. The other half is DBM and other DSPs, networks, etc. This is the half that pubs feel they can influence and put "in play" -- mess with floors, offer private auctions, pitch agencies & DSPs, cut programmatic deals, etc. From Eisar's numbers that non-GDN AdX is around $700m, versus $2-$2.5B on all the other exchanges. In other words, ~75-80% of "in play" demand is on other exchanges who offer lax policies, full bid landscapes, lower revshares, run auctions we think are bad, participate in header bidding, etc. This gives pubs good reason to work with lots of exchanges. If you buy this logic, the track two projects we are talking about should be taken in this light - not the overall size of AdX including GDN, but how do we attract more of the "in-play" demand directly onto AdX, so the pubs need the other exchanges less, and a more basic EB can be acceptable.

lessonTitle: Measure The Market You Actually Compete In
pullQuote: If you measure the whole market instead of the slice customers can actually move, you'll misjudge both your power and your problem.
situation: In October 2016, Jonathan Bellack wrote an internal email to Eisar Lipkovitz and others at Google to reframe how the company should think about AdX's competitive position. The surface question was pricing and strategy. The real question was: why do publishers keep working with rival ad exchanges instead of just using Google's?
insight: Bellack's move here is precise and underappreciated. He splits AdX's demand into two buckets: GDN (Google's own ad network — 'a giant standing demand pool' publishers can't influence) and non-GDN demand like DBM and other DSPs, which publishers *can* negotiate with, floor-price, and put 'in play.' His numbers show non-GDN AdX is roughly $700M, while competing exchanges hold $2–$2.5B of that same 'in-play' category. Translation: Google dominates the locked-down half, but rivals own 75–80% of the half publishers actually care about strategically. This is a classic competitive moat problem — but Bellack identifies that the moat protects the wrong territory. The insight driving his memo is that you can't measure your competitive strength by total volume when part of that volume is structurally captive. The real threat is in the contestable segment, and that's where rivals are winning with 'lax policies, full bid landscapes, lower revshares.' His conclusion: the team should focus 'track two projects' on pulling more in-play demand onto AdX directly, so publishers need other exchanges less.
application: Audit your product's usage by asking: which part of our volume would leave if a competitor made a better offer? That's your contestable base — and that's where your competitors are focused. Don't let a strong total number hide a weak competitive position in the segment that's actually up for grabs. Reframe your roadmap around winning that slice, not defending the captive one.
